md: ## The language that refuses to let you ship a data race

In the Go course you built the PawWalk server. Go made concurrency *easy* — `go func()` and you're done. Rust makes concurrency **safe at compile time**: the same code that would race in another language simply does not build here.

That's the pitch, and it's real. Rust gives you **C++-level performance with no garbage collector**, because memory is freed deterministically the moment its owner goes out of scope. No GC pauses. No `malloc`/`free` to get wrong. The compiler proves the lifetime for you.
> **The one-sentence pitch:** Rust makes whole classes of bugs — use-after-free, double-free, data races, iterator invalidation — *compile errors* instead of 3 a.m. production incidents.
## Where it actually runs

- **Cloud infrastructure** — AWS Firecracker (the microVM behind Lambda), Cloudflare Workers' runtime pieces, and much of the Linux kernel's new code.
- **Databases and proxies** — TiKV, Materialize, Linkerd, Deno's core.
- **CLIs** — ripgrep, fd, bat, uv, ruff. If a tool replaced something you used daily in the last five years, there's a decent chance it's Rust.
- **Product backends** — Discord, Dropbox, and Shopify run Rust services in production at very large scale.
The reason is always one of three: **speed**, **memory**, or **correctness under concurrency**. Usually all three.

md: ## The cost, stated honestly

The borrow checker will reject code that would work in other languages — and that's the point, but it *is* friction at first. You will fight it in module 02. Then something clicks and you stop fighting it, because the errors are the compiler telling you where your data flow was ambiguous.

A useful mental model: **Rust makes you design ownership before you write logic.** In dynamic languages you design the logic and discover ownership at runtime. One order produces a data race; the other produces a compile error.

**Red flag:** if you reach for `clone()` to silence the compiler, stop. That's the Rust equivalent of `.unwrap()` in production: it compiles, it runs, and it hides the design question you haven't answered.

steps.q: Which of these does Rust catch at COMPILE time that Go catches at runtime or not at all?
choices: Two threads mutating the same data without synchronisation
A misspelled function name
A type mismatch in an argument
A missing return statement
steps.explain: Go and Rust both catch typos, type mismatches, and missing returns at compile time. Data races are different: Go's race detector finds them **at runtime**, and only on the paths you actually exercised. Rust's `Send`/`Sync` rules reject the program at compile time, on every path, whether or not you wrote a test for it.
steps.nudge: Three of these are ordinary static checks almost every typed language does. One of them is Rust's whole reason to exist.

md: ## One tool to rule the build

Go shipped `go build`, `go test`, and `go mod` in one binary, and that was a revolution. Rust does the same with **cargo**, but goes further: cargo is also the **package registry client**, the **workspace manager**, the **test runner**, and the thing that runs your linters.
The four commands you'll type forever:

- **`cargo new pawwalk-api`** — scaffold a binary crate (`--lib` for a library).
- **`cargo run`** — compile and execute.
- **`cargo test`** — build and run every `#[test]`, including doctests.
- **`cargo clippy`** — the linter. It is not optional in a real project; treat its warnings as review comments.

Two more worth memorising: **`cargo fmt`** (formatting is not a debate in Rust — one canonical style) and **`cargo build --release`** (optimised build; debug builds are deliberately slow and checked).

md: ## `result` and `Option` are not exceptions

Before you write a single function, internalise this: **Rust has no exceptions.** Anything that can fail returns `Result<T, E>`, and anything that can be absent returns `Option<T>`. The compiler forces you to handle both — you cannot *forget* to check, because the value you want is wrapped inside.
let n: Option<u32> = Some(3);
let r: Result<u32, String> = Ok(3);
This is why Rust code has no `try` block around half its body. The failure path is in the type, visible at every call site.

steps.q: A function returns `Result<Walker, DbError>`. What must the caller do?
choices: Handle it — with `match`, `?`, `unwrap`, or an explicit conversion — before using the `Walker`
Nothing: errors propagate automatically like exceptions
Catch it in a `try { } catch { }` block
Declare `throws` on the calling function
steps.explain: `Result` is an ordinary enum value. The `Walker` is *inside* it; you cannot touch it without going through `match`, `if let`, `?`, or `unwrap`. The compiler guarantees you made a deliberate choice about the error.

md: ## Immutable by default
In Swift you choose between `let` and `var`. In Go you choose between `var` and `:=`. Rust flips the default: **every binding is immutable unless you write `mut`.**
let name = "Mochi";   // immutable
let mut bookings = 0;  // mutable
bookings += 1;         // fine
Try to reassign `name` and you get a compile error, not a warning. That sounds annoying until you notice how many bugs are *"something reassigned this and I didn't see where"*.
> **Pitch line:** `let` is the default, so mutability is a decision you make explicitly, at the declaration, in review.

steps.q: What does shadowing (`let x = …; let x = …;`) actually do?
choices: Creates a new binding that hides the old one; the old value is still there until it drops
Mutates the existing binding in place
Frees the old value immediately and reuses its memory
Only works for numbers
steps.explain: Shadowing creates a **new** variable. The previous one still owns its value and is dropped at the end of its scope. That's why you can shadow into a different type — `walker_name` goes from `&str` to `usize` — which a mutation could never do.

md: ## Types are inferred, but they are not optional

Rust infers types the way Swift and Go do — `let n = 5;` gives `i32` — but inference is **local and complete at compile time**. There is no dynamic typing anywhere. When inference can't decide, the compiler asks you to annotate.

The integer types you'll actually use: **`i32`** (the default, signed 32-bit), **`u32`** (unsigned — money in cents, counts), **`u64`** (ids from databases), **`usize`** (indexes and lengths). Floats: `f64`. Text: `char` is a single Unicode scalar (`'a'`), `String` is owned text, `&str` is a borrowed view — that distinction is module 02.
**Red flag:** `as` casts truncate silently. `300u32 as u8` is `44`. In production code, prefer `u32::try_from(x)?` when the value comes from outside your program.

md: ## The last expression is the return value

A Rust function body is a **block**, and a block evaluates to its last expression — provided that expression has no trailing semicolon. Add a semicolon and you turn the value into `()` (the unit type), which usually produces a type error that confuses beginners.
fn double(n: i32) -> i32 {
n * 2        // value of the block
`return n * 2;` also works, and is idiomatic for early exits. What you should *not* do is write `return` at the end of every function — in Rust the expression form is the readable default.

Functions can't return expressions
`i32` must be written as `Int32`
steps.explain: A semicolon discards the value and makes the block evaluate to `()`. The compiler then reports a type mismatch: expected `i32`, found `()`. Remove the `;` — or add `return`.

md: ## Control flow is an expression too
`if` is an expression in Rust, so it can produce a value: `let label = if n == 0 { "free" } else { "paid" };`. Both arms must have the same type.

Loops come in three flavours: **`loop`** (infinite, `break` can return a value), **`while`** (condition), and **`for`** (iterate anything implementing `IntoIterator` — ranges, vectors, maps). You will almost always want `for`.
`0..5` is a range: `0,1,2,3,4`. `0..=5` includes `5`. Ranges are values, so they compose with iterators — that's module 06.

md: ## Tuples: fixed, heterogeneous, cheap

A tuple groups values of **different** types: `let point = (3, 4);` is `(i32, i32)`. Access with `.0`, `.1` or destructure with `let (x, y) = point;`. Tuples are the idiomatic way to return two things without inventing a struct.
## Arrays: fixed, homogeneous, on the stack
An array has a **compile-time length**: `let scores = [1, 2, 3];` is `[i32; 3]`. Its type includes the length, so `[i32; 3]` and `[i32; 4]` are different types and cannot be assigned to each other.
When you need a growable, heap-allocated sequence, you want **`Vec<T>`** — that's module 06. Arrays are for fixed-size data: a colour's channels, a 4-byte header, a lookup table.

`let (x, y) = point;` works because `let` takes a **pattern** on the left. The same pattern language powers `match`, `if let`, and function arguments — module 03 leans on it hard.
This is the first place where Rust's design shows its hand: one pattern system reused everywhere, instead of a special syntax for each construct.

md: ## Everything you'll fight, in three sentences

1. **Every value has exactly one owner.**
2. **There can only be one owner at a time.**
3. **When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped.**
That's the whole system. Everything else — moves, borrows, lifetimes — is a consequence.

When you assign a heap-owning value to another binding, ownership **moves**. The old binding is not "still pointing at it"; it is now invalid, and the compiler will reject any later use. This is not a warning. It is an error.
> **Why it matters:** use-after-free is impossible because "use after move" doesn't compile. Double-free is impossible because only one owner ever drops the value.

choices: It is moved-from: the binding still exists but using it is a compile error
It is `nil`
It is an empty string

steps.explain: The binding is not deleted from the source; it becomes **moved-from**. The compiler tracks that the value is no longer there and rejects any use. There is no null and no runtime check.

md: ## `Clone` costs, `Copy` doesn't

Types that live entirely on the stack and have no destructor — integers, floats, bools, chars, and tuples/arrays of those — implement **`Copy`**. Assigning them copies the bits, and the original stays usable.

Everything else (anything owning heap memory: `String`, `Vec<T>`, `HashMap`) is only **`Clone`**: you must call `.clone()` explicitly, and you pay for the allocation. That's deliberate — Rust refuses to make an expensive copy look free.
**Red flag:** a `.clone()` sprinkled to satisfy the compiler is usually a missing borrow or a missing ownership decision. It's fine at the edges of a request; it's a smell in a hot loop.

steps.q: Which of these is `Copy`?
choices: `(i32, bool)`
`String`
`Vec<u8>`
`HashMap<String, u32>`
steps.explain: A tuple of `Copy` types is itself `Copy`, so assigning it duplicates the value and both bindings stay usable. The other three own heap memory and implement `Clone`, not `Copy`.
steps.nudge: Which one can be duplicated by copying a handful of bytes with no allocation?

md: ## Move only when you mean it
Passing ownership on every call would make Rust unusable — every function would consume your data. The fix is **borrowing**: hand out a reference instead of the value.

- **`&T`** — a shared (read-only) borrow. Many can exist at once.
- **`&mut T`** — an exclusive (read-write) borrow. **At most one** at a time, and nothing else may read it meanwhile.
That single rule — *aliasing XOR mutation* — is what eliminates data races. A data race needs two writers, or a writer and a reader, at the same time. Rust forbids exactly that shape, statically.
> **The line to remember:** many readers, or one writer. Never both.

steps.title: src/main.rs
steps.caption: `describe` borrows immutably; `rename` borrows mutably. The mutable borrow ends the moment the call returns, so the later `println!` is legal.

steps.q: How many `&mut` borrows of the same value can be alive at once?
choices: Exactly one
As many as you like, as long as you don't read through them
Two, one per thread
Unlimited in single-threaded code
steps.explain: One exclusive borrow, period. That's what makes `&mut` safe to hand to another thread: if only one mutable reference can exist, no two threads can be writing through different pointers to the same data.
steps.nudge: The rule is *aliasing XOR mutation* — no exceptions.

md: ## The borrow ends where it's last used
Older Rust required a borrow to end at the closing brace. Since **non-lexical lifetimes** (2018), a borrow ends at its **last use**, which is why this compiles:
let mut v = vec![1, 2, 3];
let first = &v[0];
println!("{first}");   // last use of the borrow
v.push(4);              // mutable borrow — legal
This is the single most useful ergonomic change Rust has shipped: the checker reasons about *what you actually do*, not about braces.

md: ## Two string types, one job each

- **`String`** — owned, growable, heap-allocated. UTF-8. You own it, you can mutate it.
- **`&str`** — a borrowed view into string data someone else owns. A `&str` is a pointer plus a length; copying it is free.
So: **function parameters take `&str`; structs that own text store `String`.** A `&str` parameter accepts both `&String` and string literals, which is why it's the flexible choice.
## Slices are the same idea for any sequence
`&v[1..3]` is a **slice** — a borrowed view into part of a `Vec`, array, or string. It's a pointer plus a length stored on the stack; no copy of the elements.

steps.explain: Lifetime **elision** covers this exact case: one input reference and one output reference means the output borrows from the input. You only write lifetimes when there is genuine ambiguity (multiple inputs, or a struct holding a reference).

md: ## Non-UTF-8 boundaries are a runtime check

Rust strings are UTF-8, so slicing by **byte index** panics if you split in the middle of a multi-byte character: `&"á"[0..1]` panics. For user-facing text, iterate characters or use `char_indices()`.

**Production habit:** `&str` for input, `String` for storage, and `Cow<'_, str>` when a function sometimes needs to allocate and sometimes doesn't. If you see `to_string()` in a hot path, ask whether a `&str` would do.

md: ## Data and behaviour, separated but named
A `struct` declares fields. An `impl` block attaches functions to it. There are no classes and no inheritance — this is the whole mechanism, and it scales further than it sounds.
Two kinds of function live in an `impl`:

- **Methods** take `self`, `&self`, or `&mut self` as the first parameter: `fn price_label(&self) -> String`.
- **Associated functions** take no `self` and are called with `::`: `Walker::new(...)`, the idiomatic constructor.
`&self` borrows, so calling a method does not move the value. That's what lets you call ten methods in a row.

steps.q: What is the difference between `fn new(...) -> Self` and `fn price_label(&self) -> String`?
choices: `new` is an associated function called as `Walker::new`; `price_label` is a method called on a value
`new` is a constructor enforced by the compiler; `price_label` is a normal method
`new` is private; `price_label` is public
There is no difference — both are methods
steps.explain: The presence of a `self` parameter is what makes something a *method* (called `value.method()`). Without it, it's an **associated function**, called with `Type::function()`. `new` is a convention, not a keyword.

md: ## Derives are the boring superpower
`#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]` generates those trait implementations for you. In a real service you'll almost always want:

- **`Debug`** — so `{:?}` works and errors are readable.
- **`Clone`** — when the value is genuinely cheap to duplicate or you need it in two places.
- **`PartialEq`** — so tests can `assert_eq!`.
Serde's `Serialize`/`Deserialize` join that list the moment the type crosses an HTTP or database boundary — that's module 10.

md: ## Enums here are nothing like enums elsewhere
In most languages an enum is a set of named integers. In Rust an enum is a **sum type**: each variant can carry its own data.
enum Booking {
Pending,
Confirmed { at: String },
Cancelled(String),   // reason

This single feature replaces a lot of what other languages do with inheritance, `instanceof` chains, and nullable fields. A value is exactly one variant, and the compiler knows which data exists in each.
> **Pitch line:** if your API has a status field plus three optional payload fields that are only valid for some statuses, that's an enum begging to exist.

steps.caption: `match` destructures each variant and binds its data: `{ walker }` pulls a named field, `(reason)` pulls the tuple payload. No casts, no `instanceof`.

It compiles and silently does nothing for the new variant

It falls through to the first arm
steps.explain: `match` must be **exhaustive**. Adding a variant breaks every `match` that doesn't handle it — at compile time, at every call site. That's the feature: the compiler hands you the complete list of places to update.
steps.nudge: Rust will not let you forget a case.

md: ## `match` is an expression with guards and bindings

Arms can have guards (`n if n > 0 =>`), range patterns (`1..=5 =>`), and nested patterns (`Some(Ok(v)) =>`). Because it's an expression, `match` produces a value and every arm must have the same type.

**Avoid `_ =>` in domain code.** A catch-all silently absorbs future variants and destroys the exhaustiveness benefit you just paid for. Use it for genuinely open sets (characters, raw input), not for your own enums.

md: ## Null, but you can't forget it
`Option<T>` is an enum: `Some(T)` or `None`. There is no null anywhere in Rust, so an absence is always visible in the type.

`Result<T, E>` is the same idea for failure: `Ok(T)` or `Err(E)`. Together these two enums replace null, exceptions, and sentinel return values — one mechanism, checked by the same exhaustiveness rule you just used.
`if let` and `while let` are the shorthand for "I only care about one variant":
if let Some(walker) = walkers.first() {
println!("{}", walker.name);

steps.q: What does `Option<usize>` communicate that `usize` with a sentinel like `-1` cannot?
choices: That absence is a real case the caller must handle, enforced by the compiler
That the value is stored on the heap
That the value can be null at runtime
Nothing — it's equivalent
steps.explain: With a sentinel, forgetting to check is a silent bug. With `Option`, forgetting is a compile error, and the type documents the possibility at every call site. There is no null pointer to dereference.

md: ## Combinators instead of pyramids
You don't have to `match` every time. `Option` and `Result` carry methods that compose: `map`, `and_then`, `unwrap_or`, `unwrap_or_else`, `ok_or`, `filter`.
let cents = parse_price(raw).ok()?;          // Option<u32>

md: ## Interfaces, minus the inheritance

A **trait** describes behaviour a type can provide. It's the closest thing Rust has to an interface, but there's no class hierarchy and no `extends` — a type implements traits independently, and you can implement a trait you own on a type you didn't write.
pub trait Priced {
fn price_cents(&self) -> u32;
fn price_label(&self) -> String {
format!("{} / 30 min", self.price_cents() / 100)
`price_label` has a **default implementation** built on `price_cents`. Implement the required method and you get the derived one for free — and any type can override it.
> **Pitch line:** a trait is a contract plus default behaviour, and the compiler checks the contract at every call site.

md: ## Coherence: one implementation per type

Rust enforces **coherence**: for a given trait and type, there is exactly one implementation, and it must live either in your crate or with your type. This is what makes method resolution predictable — the compiler never has to guess between two candidate impls.

The practical consequence: you can add `impl std::fmt::Display for Walker` in your crate, but you cannot add it for `String`, because both the trait and the type are foreign. That's the **orphan rule**, and it exists to keep downstream code from changing meaning when a dependency updates.

md: ## Generics are monomorphised, not boxed

A generic function is compiled once **per concrete type** it's used with. `largest::<i32>` and `largest::<f64>` produce two specialised functions — no boxing, no dynamic dispatch, no runtime cost versus writing them by hand.

That's why the bound matters: to call `>` on `T`, the compiler needs to know `T` supports comparison. The bound **`T: PartialOrd`** is that knowledge, and it's checked when the function is instantiated.
fn largest<T: PartialOrd + Copy>(items: &[T]) -> T
Read the bound as a requirement list: *"give me any `T` that can be ordered and copied"*.

To make the function allocate less

md: ## `impl Trait` in argument and return position
Two shorthand forms you'll see everywhere in modern Rust:

- **Argument position:** `fn log(value: impl Display)` is sugar for a generic parameter with a bound. Each call site gets its own monomorphised copy.
- **Return position:** `fn walkers() -> impl Iterator<Item = Walker>` means "some concrete type that implements this trait, which I'm not naming". The caller can use it but can't depend on the concrete type.
Return-position `impl Trait` is how libraries hand you iterators without leaking their internal types — and it keeps the door open to change them later.

md: ## Two ways to be polymorphic

- **Generics** (`T: Trait`) — *static dispatch*. The concrete type is known at compile time, the call is inlined or direct. Fastest, but the code is duplicated per type and the type must be known.
- **Trait objects** (`Box<dyn Trait>`, `&dyn Trait`) — *dynamic dispatch*. The concrete type is erased behind a pointer plus a vtable. One copy of the code, a pointer indirection per call, and you can mix types in one collection.
The rule: **use generics by default; reach for `dyn` when you need a heterogeneous collection or a runtime-chosen implementation.**
> **Pitch line:** `dyn` is not "slow" — it's a vtable hop. Use it when the alternative is a giant `match` over variants or a duplicated code path per type.

md: ## Object safety

Not every trait can become `dyn Trait`. A trait is **object safe** when its methods don't return `Self`, don't have generic parameters, and don't require `Self: Sized`. That's why `Iterator` itself isn't used as `dyn Iterator` — you write `Box<dyn Iterator<Item = T>>` with the associated type pinned.

**Production note:** prefer an enum when the set of variants is closed and known (your own domain), and `dyn` when the set is open (plugins, user-supplied handlers). An enum gives exhaustive matching; `dyn` gives extensibility.

md: ## Errors are values, and they have a shape
`Result<T, E>` is `Ok(T)` or `Err(E)`. There is no stack unwinding, no `throws`, no invisible control flow. A function that can fail says so in its signature, and the caller must deal with it.
`panic!` exists, but it is for **bugs**, not for expected failures. A missing file, bad JSON, a failed query — those are `Err`. A violated invariant your code promised — that's a panic.
> **The line:** `panic!` when the program is broken; `Result` when the world is.

md: ## `?` has a type requirement

The error type of the expression must convert into the function's error type. Either they're the same type, or `From` is implemented. That's why the `?` operator composes so well with custom error enums: you implement `From<io::Error>` once and every `io` call in the function becomes a `?`.
**Red flag:** `unwrap()` in a request handler. It turns every expected failure into a 500 and a panicking thread. Reserve `unwrap` for tests, prototypes, and cases you can prove are infallible.

md: ## The two you'll use daily

- **`Vec<T>`** — growable array on the heap. `push`, `pop`, `len`, indexing, iteration. This is the default sequence.
- **`HashMap<K, V>`** — hash map from `std::collections`. Note the import: the standard library does not put it in the prelude, unlike `Vec`.

md: ## Choosing the collection

- Need an ordered sequence with fast append and index? **`Vec`**.
- Need lookup by key? **`HashMap`** (unordered).
- Need keys in sorted order? **`BTreeMap`**.
- Need a set? **`HashSet`** / **`BTreeSet`**.
- Need a queue? **`VecDeque`**.

md: ## Iterators are lazy and free

An iterator chain does **nothing** until a consumer runs it. `iter().map(f).filter(g)` merely builds a value describing the work; `.collect()`, `.sum()`, `.count()`, or a `for` loop actually executes it.

That laziness is why chains compile down to a plain loop — no intermediate `Vec` per step, no allocation per stage. Zero-cost abstraction is not a slogan here; it's the optimizer consuming the state machine.
Three starting points, and the difference matters:

- **`iter()`** → yields `&T`.
- **`iter_mut()`** → yields `&mut T`.
- **`into_iter()`** → yields `T`, consuming the collection.

- **Select:** `filter`, `filter_map`, `take`, `skip`, `take_while`.
- **Reduce:** `fold`, `sum`, `count`, `min`, `max`, `collect`.
- **Peek:** `any`, `all`, `find`, `position`.
`filter_map` is the one people forget: it filters and maps in a single step, which is exactly what you want when the transform returns `Option`.

md: ## Closures capture, functions don't
A closure is an anonymous function that can **capture** variables from its environment. `|x| x + offset` remembers `offset` without you passing it in.
Rust infers the closure's type once, from first use — which is why you can't call the same closure with an `i32` and then a `&str`.
Three traits describe how a closure captures, and they're the vocabulary of every API that takes a callback:

- **`Fn`** — borrows immutably; callable many times concurrently.
- **`FnMut`** — borrows mutably; callable many times, one at a time.
- **`FnOnce`** — takes ownership; callable exactly once.

By default a closure borrows. Add **`move`** and it takes ownership of what it uses — required when the closure outlives the current scope, notably when spawning a thread or an async task:

let handle = std::thread::spawn(move || println!("{name}"));
Without `move`, the thread could outlive `name`. The compiler insists you prove otherwise. You'll meet this again in module 08.

md: ## Everything is private until you say otherwise

A Rust project is a tree of **modules**. `mod walker;` declares a module; the body lives in `src/walker.rs` or `src/walker/mod.rs`. Items inside are private to that module and its children unless marked `pub`.

Visibility is granular: `pub` (everyone), `pub(crate)` (this crate only), `pub(super)` (the parent module). The default — private — is what makes refactoring safe: if it isn't `pub`, you can change it without looking for callers.
> **Pitch line:** the module tree is the API. If a type isn't reachable from `lib.rs`, it isn't part of your contract.

- **Module** — a namespace inside a crate (`mod walker;`).

md: ## Fearless concurrency, literally
`std::thread::spawn` starts an OS thread. The closure must be `move` (it takes ownership of what it uses) and its return value must be `Send` — safe to move across threads.
Sharing mutable state across threads requires exactly two pieces:

- **`Arc<T>`** — atomically reference-counted pointer, so several threads can own a share.
- **`Mutex<T>`** (or `RwLock`) — runtime locking, so only one thread mutates at a time.
`Arc<Mutex<T>>` is the canonical combination. It costs an atomic increment and a lock; the compiler guarantees you can't forget either.

md: ## Deadlocks are still your problem
Rust prevents data races, not deadlocks. `Mutex` is not reentrant: locking twice in the same thread hangs. Keep critical sections short, and don't call foreign code while holding a guard.
**Production note:** prefer message passing (next lesson) for most designs. Shared mutable state behind a mutex is correct but tends to serialize throughput — the contention becomes your bottleneck.

md: ## Don't share memory; send messages
`std::sync::mpsc` is a **multi-producer, single-consumer** channel. A thread owns its data, computes a result, and sends it. Nobody locks anything.
let (tx, rx) = mpsc::channel();
thread::spawn(move || tx.send(42).unwrap());
let value = rx.recv().unwrap();
The channel closes when every sender drops — which is what makes `rx.iter()` terminate naturally instead of spinning forever.
> **Pitch line:** ownership makes message passing the *default* concurrency style in Rust, because sending a value transfers it. The type system enforces the handoff.

md: ## Bounded channels and backpressure

`mpsc::channel()` is **unbounded** — a fast producer can exhaust memory. `mpsc::sync_channel(n)` is bounded: `send` blocks when the buffer is full, which is real backpressure rather than a slow crash.

For async code, the equivalents come from `tokio::sync::{mpsc, oneshot, broadcast, watch}`. `oneshot` is for a single reply (a request/response shape), `watch` for the latest value only, `broadcast` for fan-out.

md: ## Threads are expensive; tasks are cheap

An OS thread costs megabytes of stack and a syscall. An async **task** is a state machine on the heap — you can have hundreds of thousands. That's why an HTTP server built on async handles far more concurrent connections than one thread per request.
`async fn` returns a **future**: a value representing work that hasn't happened yet. Nothing runs until something **awaits** or **polls** it. `tokio` is the runtime that polls.
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
let value = fetch().await;
The `#[tokio::main]` attribute rewrites your `main` into a synchronous function that starts the runtime and blocks on the future.

md: ## Never block the runtime
A single tokio worker thread multiplexes many tasks. If one task blocks — `std::thread::sleep`, a synchronous file read, a CPU-heavy loop — every task on that worker stalls.

Escape hatches: **`tokio::task::spawn_blocking`** for blocking I/O, **`tokio::spawn`** for CPU work you want off the reactor, and async-aware libraries (`sqlx`, `reqwest`) instead of their blocking twins.
**Red flag:** `std::thread::sleep` inside an async fn. It compiles, it passes tests, and it silently destroys throughput under load.

md: ## Axum is a router, not a kitchen sink

Axum gives you three things and gets out of the way: a **`Router`** that maps paths to handlers, **extractors** that turn a request into typed arguments, and **responses** that turn your return value into bytes. Everything else is `tower` middleware you opt into.
A handler is any `async fn` whose arguments implement the extractor traits and whose return value implements `IntoResponse`. That's the entire mental model.
async fn health() -> &'static str { "ok" }
let app = Router::new().route("/health", get(health));

md: ## Arguments are typed requests
An extractor is a type that knows how to build itself from parts of the request. The ones you'll use constantly:

- **`Path<T>`** — typed path segments (`/walkers/{id}`).
- **`Query<T>`** — the query string, deserialised into a struct.
- **`Json<T>`** — the request body, parsed as JSON.
- **`State<S>`** — your shared application state.
- **`HeaderMap`, `TypedHeader`** — headers.

md: ## Make illegal states unrepresentable

The first design decision of a Rust service isn't the router — it's the types. A `u64` called `walker_id` and a `u64` called `booking_id` are the same type, so the compiler happily lets you pass one where the other belongs.

Parse, don't validate: convert untrusted input into a type that can only exist in a valid state, as early as possible. A `ValidatedEmail` constructor that returns `Result` means every function downstream can assume validity — no defensive re-checking.

`sqlx::PgPool` is a connection pool. Cloning it is cheap — every handler gets its own handle to the same pool, and the pool enforces a maximum concurrency instead of opening 900 connections under load.

md: ## Never store a password. Store a hash, slowly.

A password hash must be **deliberately slow** so that an attacker with the database can't brute-force it. `argon2` is the current recommendation: memory-hard, tunable, and the winner of the Password Hashing Competition.

- **Unique salt per password** — generated for you by `SaltString::generate`.
- **A slow, memory-hard algorithm** — argon2id, not SHA-256.
- **Never log the password or the hash.**

md: ## A JWT is a signed claim, not a session
A JSON Web Token carries claims (`sub`, `exp`, `role`) and a signature. The server verifies the signature on each request and trusts the payload without a database lookup.
That's the trade: **stateless and fast**, but you cannot revoke a token before it expires. That's why access tokens live minutes and refresh tokens live days.

- **`exp`** — expiry, in seconds since the epoch. Always set it.
- **`iat`** — issued at, useful for debugging.

steps.title: src/auth/jwt.rs
steps.caption: `Validation::default()` checks the signature and `exp` for you. Never decode with validation disabled — that accepts anything.

steps.q: What does `Validation::default()` verify?
choices: The signature algorithm, the signature, and the expiry (among other claims)
Only that the token is valid base64
That the user exists in the database
Nothing — you must verify manually
steps.explain: It verifies the algorithm matches an allowed one, the signature is correct for the key, and `exp` (if present) hasn't passed. It does **not** check that the user still exists — that's your handler's job.
steps.nudge: The token is signed. What does that prove?

md: ## Secrets are configuration, never constants
The signing key comes from the environment, has at least 32 bytes of entropy, and rotates on a schedule. A hard-coded secret in a repo is a full authentication bypass for anyone who reads the repo.

**Production note:** use an asymmetric algorithm (`RS256`/`ES256`) when another service must verify your tokens — it can then hold only the public key. Shared-secret `HS256` is fine when one service both issues and verifies.

steps.title: Sign the claims
prompt: Implement `issue`: build the claims and sign them with the secret.
Use `encode(&Header::default(), &claims, &EncodingKey::from_secret(secret))`.

checks.hint: Build the claims: `let claims = Claims { sub: sub.to_string(), exp };`.
Sign with `encode(&Header::default(), &claims, &EncodingKey::from_secret(secret))`.

steps.success: That's a signed, expiring token. The client carries it; the server verifies it without a session table.

md: ## One place that answers who you are

In Axum, the clean way to authenticate is an **extractor**: a type whose `FromRequestParts` implementation reads the `Authorization` header, verifies the token, and yields either a `CurrentUser` or a 401.
async fn me(user: CurrentUser) -> Json<Me> {
Json(Me { id: user.id })
The handler never parses a header. If it takes `CurrentUser`, it is authenticated — by construction. If it doesn't, it's public. That's the entire policy, visible in signatures.

steps.title: src/auth/middleware.rs
steps.caption: The rejection type is a response: `(StatusCode, &str)` implements `IntoResponse`, so a failed extraction becomes a 401 automatically.

steps.q: What is the advantage of an extractor over checking the header inside each handler?
choices: Authentication becomes a type: a handler that takes `CurrentUser` cannot forget to check
It is faster
It avoids async
It removes the need for a token
steps.explain: The check happens once, before the handler body runs. Forgetting it is impossible because the type is required to compile. That's the same "make illegal states unrepresentable" rule, applied to authorization.
steps.nudge: What does the signature prove when it compiles?

md: ## Authorization is a second question

Authentication answers *who*; authorization answers *whether*. Keep them separate: the extractor yields `CurrentUser`, then the handler or a policy function decides if that user may touch this walker or booking.

**Red flag:** ownership checks scattered across handlers (`if booking.walker_id != user.id { … }`). Extract them into one policy module, or you will miss one — and the one you miss is the vulnerability.

steps.title: Extract the bearer token
prompt: Implement `bearer_token`: return the token part of an `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header, or `None`.
Use `strip_prefix` — it does the check and the slice in one step.

checks.hint: `strip_prefix("Bearer ")` returns `Some(rest)` only when the prefix matches.

steps.success: No allocation, no panic, and the scheme check and extraction are the same operation.

md: ## Config is read once, at the edge

Environment variables are untrusted strings. Read them once at startup, parse them into typed fields, and fail fast with a message that names the variable. After that, the rest of the program uses a `Config` struct — no `env::var` calls scattered through handlers.
let port: u16 = env::var("PORT")?.parse()?;
**Red flag:** `env::var("DATABASE_URL").unwrap()` inside a request handler. It's a panic waiting for a misconfigured deploy, and it hides the dependency.

steps.title: src/config.rs
steps.caption: A default for `PORT`, a hard requirement for `DATABASE_URL`, and an error message that names the variable. This function is the only place the process environment is read.

steps.q: Why parse configuration into a typed struct at startup?
choices: A misconfiguration fails immediately with a clear message instead of at the first request
It uses less memory
Environment variables cannot be read later
It is required by tokio
steps.explain: Failing at boot is a deploy that rolls back. Failing on the first request is an outage discovered by users. Typed config also means handlers never handle strings that might be invalid.
steps.nudge: When do you want to discover a missing variable?

md: ## Structured logs, not println
`tracing` gives you spans and structured fields. Instead of `println!("request failed")`, you get a line with the method, path, status and latency — filterable and aggregatable.
tracing_subscriber::fmt()
.with_env_filter(EnvFilter::from_default_env())
.init();
`RUST_LOG=pawwalk_api=debug,tower_http=info cargo run` then changes verbosity without a rebuild. Combined with `TraceLayer`, every request gets a span automatically.

Chain `std::env::var("PORT").ok().and_then(|v| v.parse().ok()).unwrap_or(8080)`.

checks.hint: Read the variable with `std::env::var("PORT")`.
Parse inside `and_then`, returning `Option` so an invalid value also falls back.
Default to 8080 with `.unwrap_or(8080)`.

steps.success: One expression, no panic, a default that works in development and an override for production.

md: ## Killing in-flight requests is a choice

A rolling deploy sends `SIGTERM`. If the process exits immediately, every in-flight request dies mid-write. `axum::serve(...).with_graceful_shutdown(...)` stops accepting new connections and lets active ones finish.
axum::serve(listener, app)
.with_graceful_shutdown(shutdown_signal())
.await?;
Pair it with a readiness endpoint that starts returning 503 before shutdown, so the load balancer drains the instance first.

steps.title: src/main.rs
steps.caption: `select!` waits for whichever signal arrives first. The `#[cfg]` split keeps it portable: SIGTERM is Unix-only, so other platforms wait on Ctrl+C alone.

steps.q: What does graceful shutdown actually change?
choices: The server stops accepting new connections and lets in-flight requests finish
It restarts the process
It closes the database pool immediately
It cancels every request
steps.explain: It removes the listener and awaits the active connections. Requests already being served complete; no new ones start. Without it, a deploy truncates whatever was mid-flight.
steps.nudge: What happens to a request that is halfway through a write?

md: ## Order matters on the way down

Drain the listener first, then close the pool. If you close the pool while requests are still running, they fail with a confusing error. The `Arc` refcount naturally does the right thing: the last handler drops the last pool handle.

**Production note:** give the shutdown a deadline (`tokio::time::timeout`). A stuck handler should not keep the process alive forever — Kubernetes will `SIGKILL` you anyway, and now you've lost the log.

steps.title: Wait for Ctrl+C
prompt: Implement `shutdown_signal`: resolve when the user presses Ctrl+C.
Use `tokio::signal::ctrl_c().await` and handle the error with `expect`.

checks.hint: Await `tokio::signal::ctrl_c()`.
The signal future must be awaited — the function is async.
Handle the error explicitly with `expect`.

steps.success: That future is what you hand to `with_graceful_shutdown`. Ctrl+C now drains instead of killing.

md: ## One binary, no runtime
`cargo build --release` produces a single statically-linked-ish binary. No JVM, no Node, no Python interpreter. That's why Rust containers are routinely 20–50 MB and start in milliseconds.
The Dockerfile shape that matters: **build in one stage, copy the binary into a minimal runtime stage**. Never ship the toolchain.
FROM rust:1-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN cargo build --release
FROM debian:bookworm-slim
COPY --from=build /app/target/release/pawwalk-api /usr/local/bin/
CMD ["pawwalk-api"]

steps.title: Dockerfile
steps.source:
# ---- build ----
FROM rust:1.82-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app

# Cache dependencies separately from source.
COPY Cargo.toml Cargo.lock ./
RUN mkdir src && echo "fn main() {}" > src/main.rs && cargo build --release

COPY . .
RUN touch src/main.rs && cargo build --release

# ---- runtime ----
FROM debian:bookworm-slim
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends ca-certificates \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

COPY --from=build /app/target/release/pawwalk-api /usr/local/bin/pawwalk-api
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["pawwalk-api"]
steps.caption: The empty `main.rs` trick builds your dependencies in their own layer, so a source change doesn't re-download the world. `touch src/main.rs` then forces your crate to rebuild.

steps.q: Why build dependencies in a separate Docker layer before copying the source?
choices: So a source-only change reuses the cached dependency layer instead of rebuilding everything
Because Cargo requires it
To make the final image smaller
To enable debug symbols
steps.explain: Docker caches layers. If `Cargo.toml` and `Cargo.lock` are unchanged, the dependency build is a cache hit; only your crate recompiles. Without the trick, every source edit rebuilds all dependencies — minutes per iteration.
steps.nudge: Docker caches by layer. What invalidates a layer?

md: ## The release checklist

Before the first real deploy: `cargo clippy -- -D warnings`, `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo test`, a `--release` build, and one `RUST_LOG=info` run against the real database. Then the operational basics: a `/health` endpoint, structured logs, a shutdown handler, and a database URL from the environment.
**Red flag:** `unwrap()` in a request path, a secret in `Cargo.toml`, or a `println!` where a `tracing` span belongs. Each one is a future incident with a timestamp.
